cases.presenting_complaint: Severe mood swings with 5 distinct episodes in the past 8 months - feeling 'like I'm on a rollercoaster'
cases.associated: Three depressive episodes (each lasting 2-3 weeks with severe anhedonia, suicidal thoughts) alternating with two hypomanic episodes (lasting 1-2 weeks with elevated mood, decreased sleep, impulsivity). Very brief euthymic periods. Exhausted by rapid shifts
cases.risk_factors: Bipolar II diagnosed 4 years ago, started antidepressant 10 months ago (may have triggered cycling), hypothyroidism (TSH slightly elevated), female sex, high stress job
cases.mse: Appearance: Tired, appears older than age. Behavior: Normal currently. Speech: Normal. Mood: 'Scared of the next swing, exhausted'. Affect: Anxious, mildly depressed. Thought: Demoralization about illness, worry about future episodes. Perception: Normal. Cognition: Intact. Insight: Excellent, keeps detailed mood diary
cases.investigations: Mood chart shows 5 distinct episodes in 8 months. TSH: 4.8 (upper normal/subclinical hypothyroid). Current meds: Lamotrigine 150mg, escitalopram 20mg. PHQ-9 currently: 12/27
cases.suicide_risk: High risk. Rapid cycling associated with increased suicide risk. History of multiple suicidal episodes during depressive phases. Demoralization about illness course
cases.explanation: Rapid cycling defined as ≥4 mood episodes in 12 months. More common in women and associated with antidepressant use, hypothyroidism, and worse prognosis. Antidepressants can induce or accelerate cycling in vulnerable patients. This patient's cycling began shortly after starting escitalopram, suggesting iatrogenic contribution. Subclinical hypothyroidism (TSH >4.0) can also contribute to rapid cycling and mood instability
cases.management: (1) Discontinue antidepressant (escitalopram) - evidence suggests worsens rapid cycling; (2) Optimize thyroid - increase levothyroxine to target TSH <2.5; (3) Optimize mood stabilizer - increase lamotrigine to 200-300mg OR add lithium (best evidence for rapid cycling); (4) Consider atypical antipsychotic if inadequate response (quetiapine or olanzapine); (5) Strict sleep-wake schedule; (6) Social rhythm therapy (IPSRT); (7) CBT for bipolar disorder; (8) Stress management; (9) Daily mood charting; (10) Avoid triggers; (11) Regular monitoring; (12) Realistic expectations - stabilization may take 6-12 months

cases.presenting_complaint: Mood changes every few days - 'one day I'm on top of the world, next day I want to die'
cases.associated: Mood shifts every 2-4 days. Periods of elevated energy, decreased sleep, impulsivity, racing thoughts lasting 2-3 days, then crashes into depression with suicidal thoughts, hypersomnia, hopelessness for 3-4 days. Very brief or no euthymic periods. Cannot maintain work or relationships
cases.risk_factors: Bipolar I diagnosed 2 years ago, multiple medication trials, poor treatment response, cocaine and alcohol use, childhood trauma, borderline personality traits
cases.mse: Appearance: Variable depending on mood state. Currently depressed phase - disheveled. Behavior: Lethargic currently. Speech: Slow. Mood: 'I don't know who I am anymore, changes too fast'. Affect: Depressed, labile. Thought: Confusion about identity due to rapid shifts, passive suicidal ideation. Perception: Normal. Cognition: Intact. Insight: Good but overwhelmed
cases.investigations: Detailed mood diary shows cycling every 2-4 days over 3 months. Substance screen: positive for cannabis. MRI brain: normal. Thyroid, metabolic panel: normal. Multiple medication trials documented
cases.suicide_risk: Very high risk. Ultra-rapid cycling associated with severe suicide risk, impulsivity, demoralization. Multiple previous attempts during depressive crashes
cases.explanation: Ultra-rapid (ultradian) cycling: mood episodes cycling within days to weeks. More severe than rapid cycling (which is monthly). Highly treatment-resistant. May represent separate phenotype. Differential includes: borderline personality disorder (but this has distinct mood episodes, not just emotional reactivity), mixed states, or severe rapid cycling bipolar. Substance use complicates picture but pattern exists even during abstinent periods
cases.management: (1) Hospitalization for stabilization; (2) Stop any antidepressants; (3) Aggressive mood stabilization: combination therapy (lithium + valproate OR lithium + atypical antipsychotic); (4) Consider clozapine (evidence for refractory bipolar); (5) ECT if medication-refractory; (6) Address substance use - inpatient detox and addiction treatment; (7) DBT for emotion regulation and borderline traits; (8) Trauma-focused therapy when stable; (9) Ultra-strict routine and sleep schedule; (10) Intensive case management; (11) Long-term residential treatment may be needed; (12) Disability assessment; (13) Family support; (14) Realistic goals - may not achieve full remission but aim for reduced amplitude of swings

cases.presenting_complaint: Chronic mood instability with ups and downs for 'as long as I can remember' - at least since late teens
cases.associated: Periods of feeling energetic, creative, social (lasting days to weeks) alternating with periods of low mood, fatigue, pessimism (lasting days to weeks). Never severe enough to meet full episode criteria. Never symptom-free for more than 6-8 weeks. Affects relationships - 'people can't keep up with my changes'
cases.risk_factors: Father has bipolar I disorder, mother has depression, creative profession (artist), irregular lifestyle, cannabis use
cases.mse: Appearance: Appropriate. Behavior: Currently in 'up' phase - animated, energetic. Speech: Slightly increased rate. Mood: 'Good right now, but I know it'll change'. Affect: Mildly elevated. Thought: Future-oriented, some grandiosity about artistic abilities. Perception: Normal. Cognition: Intact. Insight: Good - frustrated by unpredictability
cases.investigations: Retrospective mood charting over 6 months confirms numerous periods of mild elevation and mild depression. No episode meets criteria for major depression or hypomania. TSH, metabolic panel: normal. Strong family history of bipolar disorder
cases.suicide_risk: Low-moderate. Risk of eventual progression to full bipolar disorder (15-50% lifetime risk). Impulsivity during elevated periods
cases.explanation: Cyclothymia: chronic fluctuating mood for ≥2 years with numerous periods of hypomanic symptoms and depressive symptoms that don't meet full criteria for episodes. Symptom-free intervals <2 months. Often begins adolescence/early adulthood. Represents bipolar spectrum disorder - milder but chronic. Strong family history predicts progression to bipolar I or II. Causes significant interpersonal and occupational impairment despite 'milder' symptoms due to chronicity and unpredictability
cases.management: (1) Psychoeducation about cyclothymia and bipolar spectrum; (2) Consider mood stabilizer: lithium may reduce risk of progression to bipolar disorder, lamotrigine, or valproate (controversial - some prefer psychotherapy alone if functioning acceptable); (3) AVOID antidepressants (may destabilize); (4) Psychotherapy is crucial: IPSRT (interpersonal and social rhythm therapy) to regularize routines; (5) CBT for managing mood fluctuations; (6) Lifestyle interventions: strict sleep-wake schedule, exercise, avoid alcohol/cannabis; (7) Stress management; (8) Daily mood monitoring; (9) Vocational counseling; (10) Long-term monitoring for progression; (11) Shared decision-making about medication vs psychotherapy alone; (12) Regular follow-up

cases.presenting_complaint: Severe mood swings, irritability, and depression in the week before periods, with complete resolution after menstruation starts
cases.duration: Pattern for 2 years, worsened after stopping oral contraceptives
cases.associated: Luteal phase (week before period): severe irritability, mood lability, depression, anxiety, feeling overwhelmed, breast tenderness, bloating. Symptoms start ~day 21 of cycle, peak day 26-28, resolve dramatically within 1-2 days of period starting. Symptom-free during follicular phase (days 1-14). Causes relationship conflict and work impairment
cases.risk_factors: Stopped OCP 2 years ago, history of postpartum depression, family history of PMDD in mother, high-stress job
cases.mse: Appearance: Appropriate. Currently day 5 of cycle (follicular phase) - appears euthymic. Behavior: Normal. Speech: Normal. Mood: 'Fine now, but in 2 weeks I'll be a different person'. Affect: Euthymic. Thought: No abnormality currently. Perception: Normal. Cognition: Intact. Insight: Excellent - has tracked pattern carefully
cases.investigations: Prospective daily symptom diary for 2 consecutive cycles confirms: luteal phase scores 8-9/10 for irritability, mood swings, depression; follicular phase scores 1-2/10. Clear cyclical pattern. TSH, prolactin: normal. No evidence of mood symptoms outside premenstrual period
cases.suicide_risk: Moderate risk during luteal phase. Some patients with PMDD have suicidal ideation pre-menstrually. Currently low risk (follicular phase)
cases.explanation: PMDD affects 3-8% of menstruating women. Requires prospective documentation of symptoms in relation to menstrual cycle for ≥2 cycles. Must have ≥5 symptoms (including ≥1 core mood symptom: mood lability, irritability, depression, or anxiety) that are limited to luteal phase and resolve within days of menstruation. Symptoms cause significant impairment. Pathophysiology involves abnormal sensitivity to normal hormonal fluctuations (progesterone metabolites) rather than abnormal hormone levels. Differential: premenstrual exacerbation of underlying mood/anxiety disorder (symptoms present throughout cycle, worsen premenstrually)
cases.management: (1) Confirm diagnosis with 2 cycles of prospective charting (often already done); (2) FIRST-LINE: SSRI - can use continuously (sertraline 50-150mg daily) OR luteal phase only (day 14-28 of cycle, or start when symptoms begin) - both effective; (3) Oral contraceptives: continuous regimen without placebo week (eliminates cycle) - Yaz (drospirenone) is FDA-approved for PMDD; (4) GnRH agonists for severe refractory cases (induces medical menopause, add-back HRT needed); (5) CBT focusing on coping during luteal phase; (6) Lifestyle: exercise, stress reduction, adequate sleep especially luteal phase; (7) Calcium and vitamin B6 supplementation (modest evidence); (8) NSAIDs for physical symptoms; (9) Psychoeducation and symptom tracking; (10) Adjust work/social demands during luteal phase if possible; (11) Partner/family education; (12) Regular follow-up; (13) Surgical oophorectomy only for extreme refractory cases

cases.diagnosis: Borderline Personality Disorder with Mood Instability
cases.presenting_complaint: Intense mood swings throughout the day in response to relationships and events - 'my mood changes by the hour'
cases.duration: Pattern since late teens, at least 8 years
cases.associated: Rapid mood shifts (hours) triggered by interpersonal events, fear of abandonment, impulsivity (self-harm, binge eating, spending), unstable relationships, chronic emptiness, identity disturbance. Mood shifts are reactive (argument with partner → intense anger/despair → self-harm → calm)
cases.risk_factors: Childhood sexual abuse, multiple family disruptions, previous suicide attempts (3), chronic self-harm (cutting), unstable housing and employment, substance use
cases.mse: Appearance: Multiple healed scars on forearms. Behavior: Dependent, seeks reassurance. Speech: Normal but emotional. Mood: 'It depends - right now okay, but if you reject me I'll crash'. Affect: Reactive, shifts during interview from euthymic to tearful to angry. Thought: All-or-nothing thinking, intense fear of abandonment. Perception: Transient stress-related dissociation. Cognition: Intact. Insight: Variable
cases.investigations: Detailed assessment confirms 7/9 BPD criteria. Mood diary shows multiple shifts per day, always triggered by interpersonal events or perceived rejection. No clear discrete mood episodes. Substance screen: positive for cannabis. Previous diagnoses: bipolar disorder (incorrect), ADHD, depression
cases.suicide_risk: High risk. 10% lifetime suicide completion rate in BPD. Multiple previous attempts, chronic self-harm, impulsivity. Risk elevated during relationship crises
cases.explanation: BPD mood instability differs from bipolar disorder: (1) Rapid shifts (hours not days/weeks); (2) Reactive to external events especially interpersonal; (3) Baseline of chronic emptiness (not euthymia); (4) No discrete episodes with neurovegetative symptoms; (5) Part of pervasive pattern with identity disturbance, unstable relationships, impulsivity, self-harm. Often misdiagnosed as bipolar. Can have comorbid bipolar but this presents as distinct episodic pattern superimposed on BPD baseline. BPD mood instability represents emotional dysregulation not bipolar diathesis
cases.management: (1) Psychotherapy is PRIMARY treatment: DBT (Dialectical Behavior Therapy) - gold standard, addresses emotion regulation, distress tolerance, interpersonal effectiveness; OR MBT (Mentalization-Based Therapy); OR Schema Therapy; (2) AVOID labeling as 'bipolar' - worsens identity confusion and leads to inappropriate medications; (3) NO mood stabilizers or antipsychotics long-term (limited evidence, significant side effects) unless comorbid disorder; (4) Short-term SSRI for comorbid depression/anxiety; (5) Crisis management plan for self-harm urges; (6) Address trauma when stable (trauma-focused CBT or EMDR); (7) Substance use treatment; (8) Case management for housing, vocational rehabilitation; (9) NO benzodiazepines (abuse potential, disinhibition); (10) Consistent therapeutic relationship; (11) Set clear boundaries; (12) Family therapy/psychoeducation; (13) Long-term treatment (2-3 years DBT); (14) Prognosis better than historically thought - many improve significantly with treatment

cases.presenting_complaint: New onset of mood swings, irritability, and tearfulness over past 8 months along with irregular periods and hot flashes
cases.associated: Previously stable mood, now experiencing unpredictable mood swings, irritability (especially with family), tearfulness, anxiety, poor sleep (hot flashes waking her), reduced libido, difficulty concentrating. Irregular menstrual periods (every 2-6 weeks). No previous psychiatric history
cases.risk_factors: Perimenopausal (age 51, irregular periods), no psychiatric history, family history of difficult menopause in mother, recent stress (aging parents)
cases.mse: Appearance: Appropriate, appears tired. Behavior: Normal. Speech: Normal. Mood: 'Irritable, not myself'. Affect: Mildly labile, some irritability. Thought: Attributes symptoms to menopause, worried about mental health. Perception: Normal. Cognition: Subjective concentration difficulties. Insight: Good
cases.investigations: FSH: 45 IU/L (elevated, consistent with perimenopause). Estradiol: low-normal and fluctuating. TSH: normal (important to check). PHQ-9: 9/27 (mild depression). No previous psychiatric diagnoses. Temporal correlation with menstrual irregularity and vasomotor symptoms
cases.suicide_risk: Low risk. Distressed by symptoms but no suicidal ideation
cases.explanation: Perimenopause (transition to menopause) typically occurs 45-55 years. Characterized by irregular periods, fluctuating estrogen levels, and various symptoms including mood changes. Mood symptoms in perimenopause include: irritability, mood lability, anxiety, depression, poor concentration. Mechanisms: estrogen fluctuations affect serotonin, GABA, and other neurotransmitter systems; sleep disruption from hot flashes; psychosocial factors (aging, empty nest, caregiving). Risk increased in women with previous mood disorders, but can occur in those without psychiatric history. Distinguish from: primary mood disorder, thyroid dysfunction, other medical causes
cases.management: (1) Psychoeducation about perimenopause and mood symptoms; (2) FIRST-LINE for moderate-severe symptoms: Hormone Replacement Therapy (HRT) - estrogen-progesterone if intact uterus OR estrogen alone if post-hysterectomy; improves mood, vasomotor symptoms, sleep; (3) If HRT contraindicated or declined: SSRI/SNRI (effective for both mood and hot flashes) - e.g., venlafaxine 75mg, paroxetine 10-20mg, escitalopram 10mg; (4) Lifestyle interventions: regular exercise, stress management, good sleep hygiene, limit alcohol/caffeine; (5) CBT for menopause (addresses mood and hot flashes); (6) For severe vasomotor symptoms: gabapentin 300-900mg or clonidine; (7) Vaginal estrogen for genitourinary symptoms; (8) Address other stressors (aging parents - respite care, family meeting); (9) Reassurance - symptoms usually improve post-menopause; (10) Consider bone density scan if starting HRT or if risk factors; (11) Regular follow-up; (12) Adjust treatment as transitions to post-menopause (typically within 2-4 years)

cases.diagnosis: Bipolar II with Rapid Mood Changes
cases.presenting_complaint: Frequent mood shifts between depression and elevated mood with 7 episodes in past 14 months
cases.associated: Four depressive episodes (each 2-4 weeks: anhedonia, fatigue, suicidal thoughts) and three hypomanic episodes (each 4-6 days: elevated mood, decreased sleep, increased productivity, impulsivity). Brief euthymic periods. Exhausting pattern
cases.risk_factors: Bipolar II diagnosed 3 years ago, initially well-controlled on lamotrigine, started antidepressant 18 months ago, work stress increased, inadequate sleep due to shift work
cases.mse: Appearance: Appropriate. Currently in mild depressive state. Behavior: Reduced energy. Speech: Normal. Mood: 'Down again, here we go'. Affect: Depressed, frustrated. Thought: Demoralization about accelerated cycling, worry about work performance. Perception: Normal. Cognition: Reduced concentration. Insight: Excellent
cases.investigations: Detailed mood chart confirms 7 episodes in 14 months (rapid cycling). Sleep log shows irregular sleep-wake pattern due to shift work. Current medications: Lamotrigine 200mg, sertraline 100mg. Lithium level: not on lithium
cases.suicide_risk: High risk. Rapid cycling associated with increased suicide risk. History of multiple suicidal crises during depressive episodes
cases.explanation: Rapid cycling (≥4 episodes/year) in Bipolar II. Risk factors include: antidepressant use (sertraline added 18 months ago, timing correlates with cycle acceleration), circadian disruption (shift work), female sex (though this patient male). Antidepressants can induce/accelerate cycling especially without adequate mood stabilizer coverage. Shift work disrupts circadian rhythms which are fundamental to mood stability in bipolar disorder
cases.management: (1) Discontinue antidepressant (sertraline) - strong evidence worsens rapid cycling; (2) Optimize mood stabilizer: add lithium (best evidence for rapid cycling, target 0.8-1.2) OR increase lamotrigine to 300-400mg OR add valproate; (3) Address circadian disruption: change to regular daytime shift if possible (occupational health involvement), or if shift work unavoidable: bright light therapy, melatonin, strict sleep hygiene; (4) Consider adding atypical antipsychotic if inadequate response (quetiapine 200-400mg for bipolar depression); (5) Intensive psychotherapy: IPSRT (interpersonal and social rhythm therapy) focusing on regularizing daily routines; (6) CBT for bipolar disorder; (7) Daily mood and sleep monitoring; (8) Stress management; (9) Avoid alcohol, caffeine, other stimulants; (10) Regular exercise same time daily; (11) Vocational counseling regarding shift work; (12) Close monitoring initially (every 2 weeks); (13) Realistic expectations - may take 6-12 months to stabilize; (14) Long-term maintenance treatment

cases.diagnosis: Mood Reactivity in Complex Life Stressors
cases.presenting_complaint: Mood varying day-to-day based on ongoing stressful situations for past 4 months
cases.associated: Mood fluctuates with daily stressors: feel okay on good days (when partner supportive, work manageable), feel overwhelmed and tearful on bad days (partner drinking, work deadlines). Not discrete episodes, no neurovegetative symptoms, reactive mood. Chronic anxiety and sleep disturbance throughout
cases.risk_factors: Partner with alcohol problem (unpredictable behavior), work stress (risk of redundancy), financial difficulties, caring for elderly mother with dementia
cases.mse: Appearance: Tired, appropriate. Behavior: Anxious. Speech: Normal. Mood: 'Depends on the day - some days I cope, some days I can't'. Affect: Reactive, some tearfulness when discussing stressors. Thought: Overwhelmed, worry about multiple domains, no hopelessness. Perception: Normal. Cognition: Some concentration difficulty. Insight: Good - recognizes stress is the problem
cases.investigations: PHQ-9: 11/27 (varies 8-14 depending on day assessed). GAD-7: 12/21 (moderate anxiety). No evidence of discrete mood episodes on detailed history. Assessment of stressors confirms ongoing multiple chronic stressors
cases.suicide_risk: Low risk. No suicidal ideation. Good coping mechanisms when not overwhelmed
cases.explanation: This represents normal mood reactivity to severe chronic stress (adjustment disorder with mixed anxiety and depressed mood) rather than primary mood disorder. Key features distinguishing from bipolar/mood disorder: (1) Mood clearly reactive to external events; (2) No discrete episodes with clear beginning/end; (3) No neurovegetative symptoms (sleep disturbance present but due to anxiety/worry); (4) No elevated mood periods; (5) Context of overwhelming chronic stressors. Many patients and clinicians mistake stress-related mood fluctuations for bipolar disorder, leading to inappropriate treatment. This requires addressing life circumstances, not mood stabilizers
cases.management: (1) DO NOT diagnose or treat as bipolar disorder - would be harmful misdiagnosis; (2) Problem-focused therapy: identify modifiable stressors and develop action plan; (3) Partner's alcohol use: Al-Anon referral, couple therapy if partner engaged, boundaries and safety planning; (4) Work stress: occupational health referral, CV preparation if redundancy likely, financial counseling; (5) Elderly mother: arrange respite care, involve social services, share care responsibilities with family; (6) Anxiety management: CBT, relaxation techniques, mindfulness; (7) Short-term SSRI may help anxiety (sertraline or escitalopram) but not primary treatment; (8) Sleep hygiene; (9) Self-care: encourage activities that reduce stress; (10) Social support mobilization; (11) Regular counseling/therapy sessions; (12) Crisis plan if situation deteriorates; (13) NO mood stabilizers or antipsychotics; (14) Follow-up: expect mood to stabilize as life circumstances improve; (15) If symptoms persist despite life improvements, reconsider diagnosis

cases.presenting_complaint: Mood swings between feeling 'amazing' and 'completely depressed' over past 6 months, associated with cocaine and alcohol use
cases.associated: Pattern: uses cocaine on weekends → elevated mood, high energy, decreased sleep, impulsivity for 1-2 days → followed by 'crash' with severe depression, fatigue, suicidal thoughts for 3-4 days → gradual recovery to normal mood mid-week → repeat cycle. Also heavy alcohol use (40-60 units/week)
cases.risk_factors: Cocaine use disorder (2-3g per week), alcohol dependence (60 units/week), social pressures (works in finance, 'party culture'), no psychiatric history when abstinent (one 6-month abstinent period 2 years ago had stable mood)
cases.mse: Appearance: Varies with cycle. Currently mid-week 'normal' phase - appears well. Behavior: Normal currently. Speech: Normal. Mood: 'Fine today, but I know Friday will start the cycle again'. Affect: Euthymic currently. Thought: Insight into cycle, ambivalence about change. Perception: Normal. Cognition: Intact. Insight: Good about pattern, poor about need for change
cases.investigations: Urine drug screen: positive for cocaine metabolites. Blood: Elevated GGT (alcohol use). Timeline analysis clearly shows mood changes temporally related to substance use. Mood diary confirms weekly cycle correlating with weekend cocaine use and subsequent crash. No mood symptoms during previous 6-month abstinent period
cases.suicide_risk: High risk during 'crash' phase. Severe depression with suicidal ideation Monday-Wednesday post-use. Two previous attempts during crash phases
cases.explanation: Substance-induced mood fluctuations secondary to cocaine and alcohol. Cocaine causes acute dopamine surge (euphoria, elevated mood) followed by depletion during withdrawal (anhedonia, depression, fatigue). Alcohol is CNS depressant contributing to mood instability. Pattern is predictable and tied to substance use. Critical distinction from primary bipolar disorder: (1) Temporal relationship with substance use; (2) Previous sustained abstinence without mood symptoms; (3) Predictable pattern (weekend use → crash → recovery); (4) Symptoms resolve with sustained abstinence. This is NOT bipolar disorder and should not be treated with mood stabilizers
cases.management: (1) DO NOT diagnose as bipolar disorder - contraindicated and distracts from real problem; (2) Address substance use (PRIMARY issue): comprehensive assessment using AUDIT and drug use questionnaire; (3) Motivational interviewing to enhance readiness for change; (4) Detailed psychoeducation about cocaine neuropharmacology and mood effects; (5) Detoxification: may need medically supervised alcohol detox (assess withdrawal risk); (6) Addiction treatment: residential rehab vs intensive outpatient depending on severity; (7) Pharmacotherapy: consider naltrexone for alcohol, no specific medication for cocaine but treat comorbidities; (8) Cognitive-behavioral therapy for substance use; (9) Address workplace culture - may need job change; (10) Peer support (NA, CA, SMART Recovery); (11) Crisis management during crash phases (short-term, not mood stabilizer); (12) Treat residual mood symptoms only after 4-6 weeks sustained abstinence; (13) Likely mood will normalize completely with sustained abstinence; (14) Long-term recovery support; (15) Monitor closely - high relapse risk

cases.presenting_complaint: Daily mood fluctuations with irritability and emotional overreactivity since childhood, worsened in adulthood
cases.associated: Rapid mood shifts (minutes to hours) in response to frustrations or stimulation, low frustration tolerance, emotional overreactivity (rage episodes, then quick return to baseline), inattention, impulsivity, hyperactivity, difficulty sustaining attention at work, relationship difficulties due to emotional reactivity
cases.risk_factors: ADHD diagnosed in childhood, discontinued medication in teens, academic and occupational underachievement, family conflict
cases.mse: Appearance: Restless, fidgety. Behavior: Difficulty sitting still during interview, easily distracted. Speech: Sometimes rapid, interrupts. Mood: 'Frustrated, things set me off easily'. Affect: Labile, reactive to interview topics. Thought: No clear mood episodes, racing thoughts. Perception: Normal. Cognition: Inattention evident, working memory difficulties. Insight: Variable
cases.investigations: ADHD rating scales confirm persistent ADHD symptoms. Detailed history: no discrete mood episodes, mood changes are rapid (minutes-hours) and reactive. Childhood records document ADHD diagnosis age 8. No family history of bipolar disorder. Conners Adult ADHD Rating Scale: elevated
cases.suicide_risk: Low-moderate risk. Impulsivity increases risk, but no persistent suicidal ideation
cases.explanation: Emotional dysregulation is core feature of ADHD, present in 30-70% of adults with ADHD. Characterized by rapid mood shifts (minutes to hours), low frustration tolerance, emotional overreactivity, quick return to baseline. Often misdiagnosed as bipolar disorder. Key distinctions: (1) Mood shifts are very rapid (minutes-hours not days-weeks); (2) No discrete episodes with neurovegetative symptoms; (3) Reactive to immediate frustrations/stimulation; (4) Lifelong pattern consistent with ADHD; (5) Core ADHD symptoms prominent (inattention, hyperactivity, impulsivity); (6) Mood improves with ADHD treatment. Comorbid bipolar disorder can occur but is separate pattern superimposed
cases.management: (1) Treat ADHD (PRIMARY treatment for mood symptoms): Stimulant medication (methylphenidate or amphetamine) - improves mood regulation in addition to core ADHD symptoms; OR atomoxetine if stimulants contraindicated; (2) DO NOT use mood stabilizers or diagnose bipolar - inappropriate and misses actual problem; (3) CBT adapted for ADHD - organization, time management, emotional regulation strategies; (4) Behavioral interventions: identify triggers, anger management, frustration tolerance training; (5) Psychoeducation about ADHD and emotional dysregulation; (6) Lifestyle: regular sleep, exercise, structured routine; (7) Vocational rehabilitation - may need accommodations; (8) Relationship counseling - partner education about ADHD; (9) Avoid substances; (10) Regular monitoring and medication adjustment; (11) If mood symptoms persist despite optimized ADHD treatment, consider comorbid depression/anxiety; (12) Long-term ADHD treatment
